power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Active Health Problems in Real-World Consultations on a Purpose-Built Medical AI Platform

author.affiliation:

text.text: Description (submission field, 1-2 sentences): In 26,000 randomly sampled consultations on a free patient-facing medical AI platform, users presented with concrete clinical problems, led by symptoms such as headache and abdominal pain, and visit intentions were dominated by new or worsening conditions rather than general information seeking, reversing the rank order reported for a general-purpose assistant.
More than half of consultations were completed with structured clinical documentation, and 15% of those progressed to a completed physician telehealth visit.
Question: Do people use a purpose-built medical AI platform primarily to seek health information or to present active personal health problems?

Findings: In this retrospective cohort study of 26,000 randomly sampled consultations on a medical AI platform, 74.3% included symptom questions or health concerns and 5.0% included health information or education, reversing the rank order published for a general-purpose assistant.

Meaning: Users predominantly presented active personal health problems rather than general information requests, and purpose-built medical AI may function as an entry point to clinical care for some users.
concerns, whereas 5.0% (95% CI, 4.7%-5.2%) included health information or education, reversing the rank order published for a general-purpose assistant.
Overall, 53.9% of sampled consultations ended with a structured SOAP note, and 15.1% of those progressed to a completed physician telehealth review.
Conclusions and Relevance: Users of this purpose-built medical AI platform predominantly presented active personal health problems rather than general information requests.

Symptomdriven use, generation of structured clinical documentation, and progression to physician care suggest that purpose-built medical AI may function as an entry point to clinical care for some users.

Consumers have adopted conversational artificial intelligence (AI) for health at scale, as seen in a nationally representative survey conducted in early 2026, 32% of US adults reported using an AI chatbot for health information in the past year. 1 Adoption is occurring against a backdrop of constrained access to care, with more than 108 million Americans living in designated primary care shortage areas, 2 and adults without a usual source of primary care are 79% more likely to use chatbots for health information. 3 Nearly all evidence about this behavior comes from generalpurpose AI assistants, and it describes health conversations only in broad categories. [4] [5] [6] [7] Analyses of consumer chat logs, 8 surveys of adolescents and young adults, 9 and earlier search-engine query-log research 10 reach the same conclusion that people bring genuine clinical questions to tools not designed for clinical care.
text.formatted: Consumers have adopted conversational artificial intelligence (AI) for health at scale, as seen in a nationally representative survey conducted in early 2026, 32% of US adults reported using an AI chatbot for health information in the past year. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> Adoption is occurring against a backdrop of constrained access to care, with more than 108 million Americans living in designated primary care shortage areas, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> and adults without a usual source of primary care are 79% more likely to use chatbots for health information. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> Nearly all evidence about this behavior comes from generalpurpose AI assistants, and it describes health conversations only in broad categories. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> Analyses of consumer chat logs, <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> surveys of adolescents and young adults, <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> and earlier search-engine query-log research <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> reach the same conclusion that people bring genuine clinical questions to tools not designed for clinical care.

text.text: To our knowledge, no study has described the topics of clinical content in this demand for care.

The recent literature has characterized broad domains of health information seeking behaviors, but not the types of symptoms people ask about, the specific conditions they are concerned about, or the relevant clinical specialties.
In this study, we characterized 26,000 consultations sampled over 13 months from a patient-facing medical AI platform.

We evaluated the specific medical concepts users presented, coded to SNOMED CT, their visit intentions, classified with the same published taxonomy for contextualization with the general-purpose assistant, and rates of progression to a completed physician telehealth visit.
Doctronic operates a free, publicly available, consumer-facing, anonymous-by-default medical AI platform (www.doctronic.ai) presented as a primary care style consultation.
text.formatted: Doctronic operates a free, publicly available, consumer-facing, anonymous-by-default medical AI platform (<ref type="url" target="www.doctronic.ai">www.doctronic.ai</ref>) presented as a primary care style consultation.

text.text: It communicates that the consultation is AI and does not replace a licensed physician.

Users complete an AI consult, which is a chat conversation with the medical AI, and receive potential diagnoses, a treatment plan, and a clinically formatted SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) note to share with a healthcare provider.
Unlike an open-ended general-purpose assistant, the AI consult has a defined endpoint.

The AI continues to ask follow-up questions until it has sufficient information to summarize the history, suggest potential diagnoses, and recommend management, and the consult then concludes with generation of the note.
A consultation can end without a note if the user enters the diagnostic flow but stops answering its questions before it completes.
The AI consult is free at every step.

Users may optionally progress from the free AI consult to a telehealth visit with a licensed physician in the affiliated clinic, available in all 50 US states and the District of Columbia, for a fee of $39 that can be paid by the user directly or through health insurance.
This exploratory retrospective observational cohort study analyzed de-identified AI consult transcripts and encounter-level operational metadata (Figure 1).
text.formatted: This exploratory retrospective observational cohort study analyzed de-identified AI consult transcripts and encounter-level operational metadata (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: This study followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting guideline.
Eligible for sampling were individuals aged 18 years or older who engaged in chat with the medical AI between June 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026 (13 calendar months).

We excluded consults with fewer than five chat interaction rounds (26%), a threshold ensuring sufficient conversational content for concept and intention extraction, given briefer exchanges often do not contain enough text to determine intent.
From this population we drew a random sample of 2,000 consultations per month (26,000 in total).
Sampling managed the computational cost of extraction and represented each month equally because the platform grew rapidly over the study window.
The sample was global; device time zone region served as a coarse geographic indicator.
Age and sex were user-entered intake information.
Consultations conducted in a language other than English were excluded.

For each sampled consultation, a pipeline extracted clinical concepts from the de-identified conversation text and linked each concept to the Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine, Clinical Terms (SNOMED CT) 11 by lexical fuzzy matching, returning a concept type, clinical status, and match score against a prespecified threshold; concepts below the threshold were retained in tabulations.
text.formatted: For each sampled consultation, a pipeline extracted clinical concepts from the de-identified conversation text and linked each concept to the Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine, Clinical Terms (SNOMED CT) <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> by lexical fuzzy matching, returning a concept type, clinical status, and match score against a prespecified threshold; concepts below the threshold were retained in tabulations.

text.text: Per protocol, the SNOMED CT linkage is approximate supporting detail rather than validated clinical coding.

A structured-output large language model (LLM) pipeline identified each distinct visit intention expressed in the de-identified conversation text and returned one or more intent categories per intention from a prespecified set of 11 developed by the study authors (SG, AWL).
Intent was inferred primarily from the opening rounds of the conversation.
The pipeline was built on the GPT-4o mini model (OpenAI); the output schema was constrained to fixed enumerations, with no training or fine-tuning on study data.

To enable a rough comparison with the published characterization of a general-purpose assistant, the same consultations were reclassified using the 12-category consumer-health taxonomy of Costa-Gomes et al, with the published category definitions embedded verbatim in the classification prompt. 4
text.formatted: To enable a rough comparison with the published characterization of a general-purpose assistant, the same consultations were reclassified using the 12-category consumer-health taxonomy of Costa-Gomes et al, with the published category definitions embedded verbatim in the classification prompt. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref>

text.text: Three physician authors (SG, BJW, BC) independently annotated 200 randomly sampled study consultations, each reviewed by 1 physician on the scrubbed transcript.
Physicians assigned an intent category and a taxonomy category using the pipelines' category definitions and rated the assigned SNOMED CT concept as clinically reasonable or not appropriate.
Physician labels were the reference standard and agreement is reported as exact-match concordance with exact 95% CIs.
All data were de-identified before research use.

Free-text transcripts underwent automated scrubbing that detects and removes personally identifiable information, including names, contact details, government-issued identifiers, and financial account details.
All extraction pipelines operated on the anonymous and/or de-identified, scrubbed conversation text.
In the primary analyses, no human researcher accessed conversation content.
For the validation subsample, physician authors reviewed scrubbed, de-identified transcripts under the same access controls.
Encounter-level data elements were limited to coarse, non-identifying attributes, with ages reported in bands.
De-identification and automated scrubbing occurred within Doctroniccontrolled systems with access controls.
No attempt was made to re-identify users, and results are reported only in aggregate.
All data used in this research were collected and used in accordance with the terms of agreement with users, including as set out in the Doctronic privacy policy. 12
text.formatted: All data used in this research were collected and used in accordance with the terms of agreement with users, including as set out in the Doctronic privacy policy. <ref type="bibr">12</ref>

text.text: All analyses were descriptive and exploratory.
Distributions are reported as counts and percentages with 95% Wilson score confidence intervals on the pooled cohort over the full study window.
Taxonomy categories were tabulated at the consultation level; a consultation can express more than 1 category, so shares do not sum to 100%.
Consultations whose extraction failed schema validation were excluded, with counts reported.
An AI-generated SOAP note served as the surrogate endpoint for completion of the AI visit.

For consultations with a SOAP note, we report progression to a telehealth visit at which a Doctronic Physician Group physician reviewed the note, ascertained as of July 14, 2026, with no fixed follow-up window, so later consultations had less time to progress, biasing the estimate downward.
Only visits with the affiliated clinic are observable.
Users may instead take the SOAP note to an outside clinician, so the estimate understates total progression to clinician care.
The platform sets no target for this rate.
Because each month contributed 2,000 consultations regardless of volume, pooled estimates describe a month-balanced sample rather than the volume-weighted consultation population.
Analyses used Python 3.13 (Python Software Foundation) with pandas and NumPy; validation analyses used R.
Sex, age category, and region of the 26,000 sampled medical AI consultations are reported in
Table 1.

Among the sampled consultations, 53.9% (95% CI, 53.2%-54.5%) completed the AI consult with a SOAP note summary, and 15.1% (95% CI, 14.6%-15.7%) of those with a SOAP note proceeded to a telehealth visit with a physician.
Because the affiliated clinic operates only in the United States, this estimate also includes non-US users who could not progress to the affiliated telehealth clinic.
The SNOMED CT pipeline extracted 77,597 clinical concepts from 25,975 consultations (25 extraction failures excluded), a mean of 3.0 concepts per consultation.

The largest clinical family topic areas were gastrointestinal (15.4% of consultations), musculoskeletal and limb (15.0%), neurologic (13.2%), general and constitutional (13.0%), and sexual and reproductive health (12.6%), with skin, hair, and nail concerns close behind (10.4%).
Presenting symptoms led the demand from headache, abdominal pain, fatigue, and fever as the most frequently extracted concepts.

Some clinical topic areas were distributed with a long tail of diverse clinical concepts (eg, sexual and reproductive health), while other areas focused on a few specific concepts (eg, neurologic) (Figure 2).
text.formatted: Some clinical topic areas were distributed with a long tail of diverse clinical concepts (eg, sexual and reproductive health), while other areas focused on a few specific concepts (eg, neurologic) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: The mean lexical match score was 0.95, with 2.8% of concepts below the prespecified 0.7 threshold.

The intent extraction pipeline processed 25,975 consultations (25 extraction failures excluded) and identified 55,348 distinct visit intentions (median, 2 per consultation [IQR, 1-3]); 91 unclassifiable intentions were excluded from denominators.

A new or worsening condition was the most common first-listed intention, accounting for 60.1% (95% CI, 59.7%-60.5%) of 55,257 classified intentions, followed by health education requests (17.8% (95% CI, 17.5%-18.1%)) and reassurance seeking (7.7% (95% CI, 7.5%-7.9%)); the distribution across all 11 prespecified categories is shown in Figure 3.
text.formatted: A new or worsening condition was the most common first-listed intention, accounting for 60.1% (95% CI, 59.7%-60.5%) of 55,257 classified intentions, followed by health education requests (17.8% (95% CI, 17.5%-18.1%)) and reassurance seeking (7.7% (95% CI, 7.5%-7.9%)); the distribution across all 11 prespecified categories is shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>.

text.text: When the same consultations were reclassified with the published 12-category consumer-health taxonomy, the rank order of categories reversed relative to that published for the general-purpose assistant.

We found 74.3% (95% CI, 73.8%-74.8%) of 25,998 classified consultations (2 classification failures excluded) included at least 1 intention in Symptom Questions and Health Concerns, whereas Health Information and Education, the leading category on the generalpurpose assistant (40.7% of Copilot health-related conversations), appeared in only 5.0% (95% CI, 4.7%-5.2%).

Categories designed to capture professional and administrative uses of a generalpurpose assistant (Research and Academic Support, Medical Paperwork, Digital Tools and Fitness Apps) were sparsely populated.
The full contextualization is presented in Table 2.
text.formatted: The full contextualization is presented in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">2</ref>.

text.text: Among the 200 annotated consultations, pipeline-physician concordance was 73.5% (95% CI, 66.8%-79.5%) for the 11-category intent classification and 79.0% (95% CI, 72.7%-84.4%) for the 12-category taxonomy, comparable to the source study's 84%, with disagreements concentrated in adjacent categories.
Physicians rated the assigned SNOMED CT concept clinically reasonable in 94.8% (95% CI, 90.4%-97.6%) of consultations with an assigned concept.
Users of a purpose-built, consumer-facing medical AI platform presented with concrete clinical problems and care-seeking intent.
The most frequently extracted concepts were presenting symptoms such as headache and abdominal pain, and 3 of every 5 first-listed intentions concerned a new or worsening condition.

When re-classified with the same published taxonomy used to characterize a general-purpose assistant, we found that information seeking -dominant on the general-purpose assistant -was a small minority on the medical AI platform, where symptom questions and active health concerns dominated.

The encounters also connected to downstream clinical care: more than half of sampled consultations generated structured clinical documentation, and 15.1% of those proceeded to a completed physician review during a telehealth visit, an observable lower bound on progression to clinician care.
The transferable lesson is that the platform a person chooses may reflect their intent.
People may bring general health questions to general-purpose assistants and active personal health problems to medical AI.
Interactions on purpose-built platforms may function more like traditional care encounters and may warrant the evidence standards applied to other care settings.
This study has limitations.
First, the SNOMED CT linkage is lexical and approximate.
Physicians judged the assigned concepts clinically reasonable in most annotated consultations, but the linkage remains supporting detail rather than validated coding.

Second, the population of selfselected users of a free, anonymous platform may not be representative of the general population, and minimal demographics are collected by anonymous-by-default design, so representativeness cannot be fully assessed in this cohort.
Relatedly, the eligibility threshold of five chat interaction rounds excludes brief exchanges, which are the most likely to be purely informational.

The platform returns potential diagnoses and management recommendations only when the consult completes, users seeking a quick informational answer are likely to stop early, so the small share of information seeking partly reflects the eligibility criterion as well as the platform.
In a sensitivity analysis, 2,000 excluded consultations with fewer than five interaction rounds were processed with the same extraction pipelines.

Relative to the analytic cohort, health education requests were more common (46% vs 30%, with months weighted equally) and new or worsening conditions less common (39% vs 68%), although symptom questions and health concerns remained the most common taxonomy category (51% vs 74%).

Third, the contextualization with the prior study is a population-level contrast across platform, period, and classification pipeline rather than a measured effect; the published estimates could not be recomputed because the source data are not available.
Automated classification agreed substantially with physician annotation, but residual misclassification is possible, so the contrast supports rank order rather than magnitude.

Fourth, the anonymous-by-default design prevents linking consultations from the same individual, so a person may contribute more than 1 consultation and confidence intervals, which assume independence, may be narrow.
Finally, this analysis characterizes the demand users brought to the platform, not the clinical quality of the medical AI's responses.
Future studies from this platform will evaluate whether escalation and referral occur when clinically indicated.
In these consultations, care seeking was dominated by active personal health problems that produced structured clinical documentation and linked to downstream physician care.
These findings suggest that purpose-built medical AI may function as an entry point to care for some users. users under which they were collected.
Aggregate data supporting the findings are available in the article and its tables.
